cache-flow.title: Cache-aside pattern
cache-flow.description: The app checks the cache first and only falls back to the database on a miss

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: A user's browser or app making a request for data

nodes.label: App Server
nodes.explanation: Your application. On each read it checks the cache first; only on a miss does it query the database, then stores the result back in the cache.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.explanation: A fast in-memory store holding recently used data. Answers in microseconds when the data is present (a cache hit).

nodes.label: Database
nodes.explanation: The source of truth on disk. Slower, but always correct. Hit only when the cache misses.

load-balancer-fanout.title: One entry point, many servers
load-balancer-fanout.description: The load balancer spreads requests across identical servers and routes around unhealthy ones

nodes.label: Clients
nodes.explanation: All incoming traffic points at one address — the load balancer — instead of any individual server.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.explanation: Distributes each request across the pool of servers (e.g. round-robin or least-connections) and runs health checks so it never sends traffic to a dead server.

nodes.label: Server 1
nodes.explanation: One of several interchangeable servers running the same application code.

nodes.label: Server 2
nodes.explanation: Another identical server. If it fails a health check, the load balancer simply stops routing to it.

nodes.label: Server 3
nodes.explanation: Adding more servers behind the balancer is how the system scales horizontally.

sharding-split.title: Data split across shards
sharding-split.description: A shard key decides which database holds each row

nodes.label: Router
nodes.explanation: Application logic (or a proxy) that reads the shard key on each request and routes it to the shard that owns that data.

nodes.label: Shard A
nodes.explanation: Holds users A–H. A complete, independent database — just a slice of the whole.

nodes.label: Shard B
nodes.explanation: Holds users I–P. Its own server, CPU, and disk — so load is split, not stacked.

nodes.label: Shard C
nodes.explanation: Holds users Q–Z. Add a shard and you add capacity for both data and traffic.

cdn-edges.title: Content served from the edge
cdn-edges.description: Users hit a nearby edge server; only a miss reaches the origin

nodes.label: User (Europe)
nodes.explanation: A visitor far from your origin server. Without a CDN, every byte would travel across the world.

nodes.label: User (US)
nodes.explanation: A visitor near a different edge location, served by their own nearby copy.

nodes.label: CDN Edge
nodes.explanation: An edge server caching copies of your static assets close to users. Answers most requests itself.

nodes.label: Origin Server
nodes.explanation: Your real server. The CDN only contacts it on a cache miss, then caches the result at the edge.

read-replica-set.title: One primary, many replicas
read-replica-set.description: Writes go to the primary; reads spread across replicas

nodes.label: App Server
nodes.explanation: Sends writes to the primary and load-balances reads across the replicas.

nodes.label: Primary
nodes.explanation: The single source of truth. All writes (inserts/updates/deletes) go here.

nodes.label: Replica 1
nodes.explanation: A read-only copy kept in sync with the primary. Serves read queries to take load off it.

nodes.label: Replica 2
nodes.explanation: Another read replica. Add more to scale reads — but each lags the primary slightly.

message-queue-flow.title: Producer, queue, consumers
message-queue-flow.description: Work is buffered in a queue and processed in the background

nodes.label: Producer
nodes.explanation: The web server. Instead of doing slow work itself, it drops a message on the queue and responds immediately.

nodes.label: Queue
nodes.explanation: Holds pending jobs until a worker is free. Absorbs spikes and survives worker crashes.

nodes.label: Worker 1
nodes.explanation: Pulls jobs off the queue and processes them at its own pace.

nodes.label: Worker 2
nodes.explanation: Another consumer. Add workers to drain the queue faster when it backs up.

api-gateway-fanout.title: One front door to many services
api-gateway-fanout.description: The gateway authenticates and routes each request to the right service

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Talks to a single endpoint — the gateway — instead of knowing about every backend service.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.explanation: Handles auth, rate limiting, and routing in one place, then forwards each request to the service that owns it.

nodes.label: Users Service
nodes.explanation: Owns user accounts and profiles.

nodes.label: Orders Service
nodes.explanation: Owns orders and checkout.

nodes.label: Search Service
nodes.explanation: Owns product search.

microservices-split.title: Independent services, independent data
microservices-split.description: Each service deploys and scales on its own, with its own database

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Reaches the system through the gateway.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.explanation: Routes requests to the right service.

nodes.label: Users Service
nodes.explanation: A small, independently deployable service.

nodes.label: Orders Service
nodes.explanation: Owns its own logic and can scale separately from the others.

nodes.label: Billing Service
nodes.explanation: Owned by a different team, deployed on its own schedule.

nodes.label: Users DB
nodes.explanation: Each service keeps its own data — no shared database to couple them.

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.explanation: Private to the Orders service.

nodes.label: Billing DB
nodes.explanation: Private to the Billing service.

monolith-single.title: One deployable unit
monolith-single.description: All features live in a single application backed by one database

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Talks to one application.

nodes.label: Application
nodes.explanation: Users, orders, billing, and search all live in one codebase, deployed as a single unit. Simple to build and reason about.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.explanation: One shared database for the whole application.

event-bus.title: Publish once, react many times
event-bus.description: A publisher emits an event; interested subscribers react independently

nodes.label: Orders Service
nodes.explanation: When an order is placed it publishes an `OrderPlaced` event — it doesn't know or care who listens.

nodes.label: Event Bus
nodes.explanation: Carries events from publishers to every interested subscriber.

nodes.label: Email Service
nodes.explanation: Reacts to OrderPlaced by sending a confirmation email.

nodes.label: Inventory Service
nodes.explanation: Reacts by decrementing stock.

nodes.label: Analytics Service
nodes.explanation: Reacts by recording the sale. Add new reactions without touching the publisher.

circuit-breaker-flow.title: A breaker in front of a shaky dependency
circuit-breaker-flow.description: When failures pile up the breaker trips open and fails fast

nodes.label: Your Service
nodes.explanation: Calls a dependency through a circuit breaker instead of calling it directly.

nodes.label: Circuit Breaker
nodes.explanation: Watches the call's success rate. While the dependency is healthy it's *closed* and lets calls through; after too many failures it trips *open* and rejects calls instantly.

nodes.label: Payment API
nodes.explanation: A slow or failing third-party dependency. The breaker keeps its trouble from dragging down your service.

failover-active-standby.title: Active with a standby ready
failover-active-standby.description: If the primary fails, traffic switches to the standby

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Reaches whichever server is currently active.

nodes.label: Primary (active)
nodes.explanation: Handles all traffic today. A health check watches it constantly.

nodes.label: Standby
nodes.explanation: An idle copy kept in sync, ready to take over the moment the primary fails.

rate-limit-gate.title: A gate that caps request rate
rate-limit-gate.description: Requests within the limit pass; excess gets rejected

nodes.label: Clients
nodes.explanation: Many callers — some well-behaved, some hammering your API.

nodes.label: Rate Limiter
nodes.explanation: Counts requests per client over a time window. Within the limit, it forwards; over it, it replies `429 Too Many Requests`.

nodes.label: App Server
nodes.explanation: Protected from overload — it only sees traffic the limiter let through.

websocket-connection.title: One persistent, two-way connection
websocket-connection.description: After a handshake, both sides can push messages anytime

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Opens a WebSocket once, then keeps it open. No need to re-ask for updates.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.explanation: Holds the connection open and pushes data to the client the instant something happens.

polling-loop.title: Ask again, and again
polling-loop.description: The client repeatedly asks the server whether anything is new

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Has no way to be notified, so it asks on a timer — every few seconds — whether there's anything new.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.explanation: Answers each request. Most of the time the answer is 'nothing new', so much of the traffic is wasted.

dns-resolution.title: Name to address, then connect
dns-resolution.description: The browser asks DNS for an IP, then talks to the server directly

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.explanation: Knows the domain name but not where it lives. It must look up an IP address first.

nodes.label: DNS Resolver
nodes.explanation: Translates the human-readable domain into an IP address, caching the answer for a while (TTL).

nodes.label: Web Server (93.184.x.x)
nodes.explanation: The actual server at the resolved IP. The browser connects here once it has the address.

reverse-proxy-front.title: A proxy in front of the servers
reverse-proxy-front.description: Clients only ever talk to the proxy; it terminates SSL, caches, and forwards

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Talks only to the proxy and never sees the backend servers directly.

nodes.label: Reverse Proxy
nodes.explanation: Sits in front of the servers: terminates SSL, serves cached/static content, compresses responses, and forwards the rest. Hides and protects the backend.

nodes.label: App Server 1
nodes.explanation: A backend the client never addresses directly.

nodes.label: App Server 2
nodes.explanation: Another hidden backend. The proxy can also balance load across them.

http-req-res.title: Request, then response
http-req-res.description: The client sends a request with a method; the server replies with a status

nodes.label: Client
nodes.explanation: Sends an HTTP request naming a method (GET/POST/…) and a path.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.explanation: Processes the request and returns a status code (200, 404, 500…) plus a body. Each request stands alone — HTTP is stateless.

rpc-call.title: Call a remote function like a local one
rpc-call.description: Service A invokes a procedure on Service B and waits for the result

nodes.label: Service A
nodes.explanation: Calls `getUser(42)` as if it were a local function — the RPC framework handles packing the call and sending it over the network.

nodes.label: Service B
nodes.explanation: Runs the actual procedure and returns the result. To Service A it feels like an ordinary function call.

federation-split.title: Split the database by function
federation-split.description: One database per feature area, instead of everything in one

nodes.label: App Server
nodes.explanation: Routes each query to the database that owns that feature area.

nodes.label: Users DB
nodes.explanation: Owns everything about users — its own server, its own load.

nodes.label: Products DB
nodes.explanation: Owns the catalog. Splitting by function means each DB sees less traffic.

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.explanation: Owns orders. Unlike sharding (same data split by rows), federation splits by feature.
